A practical, indicator-first method for turning a term scheme of learning into weekly lesson plans that a teacher can actually teach and defend.
By BloomCore Technologies · 9 November 2026 · 9 min read
1. Read the scheme as a sequence, not a list
2. Map the weeks to real teaching time
3. Turn each indicator into one lesson objective

Keep the indicator reference beside the objective. It is the thread between the curriculum, the lesson and the assessment. When a supervisor asks why a topic is being taught, the answer should be visi
4. Choose teaching and learning resources that exist
Where a resource is scarce, design the lesson around groups or a demonstration. Record who carries what, so the activity does not collapse at the start of the period.

6. Review the plan against the indicator

At the end of the week, note what actually happened. Which indicator took longer? Which task produced weak evidence? Which resource failed? Carry that note into the next week's plan instead of startin
This small habit is what turns a template into professional judgement. The scheme stays stable; the plan learns from the classroom.
Common mistakes and a better habit
Copying the content standard into the objective. A standard describes the destination; an objective describes what this lesson will produce.
Planning three indicators for one period. Depth beats coverage when the indicator will be assessed.
Listing resources without checking availability. Confirm the textbook, the chart and the room before the week starts.
Leaving assessment to the end of the term. Build a small evidence point into every lesson.
Rewriting the whole scheme each week. Keep the scheme, adjust the plan.
The test of a lesson plan is simple. Could another teacher pick it up and teach the same indicator without asking what you meant? If yes, the plan is doing its job.

Recordkeeping for a mobile money business: a daily routine that works
A daily routine for mobile money agents and multi-location operators: opening position, transaction records, float and reconciliation.
By BloomCore Technologies · 9 November 2026 · 10 min read
The routine below is deliberately ordinary. It is designed to be repeated every day by people who are busy serving customers, not by an accountant at the end of the month.
If the business runs several locations, each location needs its own opening position. A single organisation-wide total hides the branch that is short.
Record the transaction, not just the total
For each transaction, capture enough detail to answer a customer query without guesswork:
Customer name or a consistent customer reference.
Transaction type: deposit, withdrawal, transfer, bill payment, airtime, or another supported service.
The location and the staff member who handled it.
A provider reference or receipt number where one exists.
The resulting cash and float position, where the system can calculate it.
Totals are a summary, not a record. If the only entry for the day is a lump sum, a customer dispute or a staff query cannot be investigated later.
Keep business money separate from personal money
Reconcile at closing, not at the end of the month
Count the cashCount the physical cash in the presence of a second person where possible, and write the figure down before checking the expected balance.
Count the physical cash in the presence of a second person where possible, and write the figure down before checking the expected balance.
Check the floatCompare the electronic balance with the platform or provider record. Note any transaction still pending.
Compare the electronic balance with the platform or provider record. Note any transaction still pending.
Explain every differenceA difference is not automatically a loss. It may be an unrecorded charge, a pending reversal or a transaction entered twice. Record the explanation and who gave it.
A difference is not automatically a loss. It may be an unrecorded charge, a pending reversal or a transaction entered twice. Record the explanation and who gave it.
Close the dayLock the day's records, carry the closing position to the next opening, and keep the summary with the transaction detail.
Lock the day's records, carry the closing position to the next opening, and keep the summary with the transaction detail.
Handle susu collections as a separate ledger
A collector's route changes. Customers miss a day. A partial payment is agreed. The record must allow those realities without losing the link between the customer and the money.
Review the week, not only the day
This review is where patterns appear. A daily difference may be an error. The same difference every Friday is a process problem.
Recording only the day's total, which makes individual transactions impossible to trace.
Letting staff share a login, which removes accountability without improving speed.
Treating float and cash as one number.
Failing to record reversals and pending transactions.
Keeping customer data in a personal phone with no backup and no access control.
Reconciling only when something goes wrong.
Good recordkeeping does not make a business slower. It makes the difficult conversation shorter, because the answer is already written down.

Stock control for electrical shops: item codes, counts and accountability
How electrical retailers can organise item codes, receiving, transfers, pricing and cycle counts so that the stock record matches the shelf.
By BloomCore Technologies · 9 November 2026 · 9 min read
The aim of stock control is not a perfect spreadsheet. It is a record that answers three questions quickly: what is here, where is it, and who moved it?
Give every item a stable code
Record the unit of measure with the code. Cable may be stocked in rolls and sold in metres. A code that does not state the unit invites a costly conversion error.
One code per sellable variant, not one code per supplier invoice line.
A description a new staff member can match to the shelf.
A unit of measure and, where relevant, the pack size.
A reorder level based on normal sales, not on a guess.
Where the same item comes from two suppliers at different costs, keep the cost attached to the receipt. A single average cost hides which supplier is actually cheaper.
Update the record at the point of sale
For items sold by length or partial quantity, record the quantity sold rather than the number of pieces. A roll of cable that leaves the store should reduce the metres, not the roll count.
Decide who may change a price. Record the old price, the new price, the date and the person who approved it. This is not bureaucracy; it is the difference between a discount and an unexplained margin
Keep a current price list where staff can see it. If a price is negotiated for a customer, record the reason and the approver.
At the start of a shift, record the opening float. At the end, count the cash and compare it with sales, refunds and any expenses paid from the till. The person responsible should sign or confirm the

A daily routine for mobile money agents and multi-location operators: opening position, transaction records, float and reconciliation.
By BloomCore Technologies · 9 November 2026 · 10 min read
The routine below is deliberately ordinary. It is designed to be repeated every day by people who are busy serving customers, not by an accountant at the end of the month.
If the business runs several locations, each location needs its own opening position. A single organisation-wide total hides the branch that is short.
Record the transaction, not just the total
For each transaction, capture enough detail to answer a customer query without guesswork:
Customer name or a consistent customer reference.
Transaction type: deposit, withdrawal, transfer, bill payment, airtime, or another supported service.
The location and the staff member who handled it.
A provider reference or receipt number where one exists.
The resulting cash and float position, where the system can calculate it.
Totals are a summary, not a record. If the only entry for the day is a lump sum, a customer dispute or a staff query cannot be investigated later.
Keep business money separate from personal money
Reconcile at closing, not at the end of the month
Count the cashCount the physical cash in the presence of a second person where possible, and write the figure down before checking the expected balance.

Check the floatCompare the electronic balance with the platform or provider record. Note any transaction still pending.

Explain every differenceA difference is not automatically a loss. It may be an unrecorded charge, a pending reversal or a transaction entered twice. Record the explanation and who gave it.

A collector's route changes. Customers miss a day. A partial payment is agreed. The record must allow those realities without losing the link between the customer and the money.

How electrical retailers can organise item codes, receiving, transfers, pricing and cycle counts so that the stock record matches the shelf.
By BloomCore Technologies · 9 November 2026 · 9 min read
The aim of stock control is not a perfect spreadsheet. It is a record that answers three questions quickly: what is here, where is it, and who moved it?
Give every item a stable code
Record the unit of measure with the code. Cable may be stocked in rolls and sold in metres. A code that does not state the unit invites a costly conversion error.
One code per sellable variant, not one code per supplier invoice line.
A description a new staff member can match to the shelf.
A unit of measure and, where relevant, the pack size.
A reorder level based on normal sales, not on a guess.
Where the same item comes from two suppliers at different costs, keep the cost attached to the receipt. A single average cost hides which supplier is actually cheaper.
Update the record at the point of sale
For items sold by length or partial quantity, record the quantity sold rather than the number of pieces. A roll of cable that leaves the store should reduce the metres, not the roll count.
Decide who may change a price. Record the old price, the new price, the date and the person who approved it. This is not bureaucracy; it is the difference between a discount and an unexplained margin
Keep a current price list where staff can see it. If a price is negotiated for a customer, record the reason and the approver.

Recordkeeping for a mobile money business: a daily routine that works
A daily routine for mobile money agents and multi-location operators: opening position, transaction records, float and reconciliation.
By BloomCore Technologies · 9 November 2026 · 10 min read
The routine below is deliberately ordinary. It is designed to be repeated every day by people who are busy serving customers, not by an accountant at the end of the month.
If the business runs several locations, each location needs its own opening position. A single organisation-wide total hides the branch that is short.
Record the transaction, not just the total
For each transaction, capture enough detail to answer a customer query without guesswork:
Customer name or a consistent customer reference.
Transaction type: deposit, withdrawal, transfer, bill payment, airtime, or another supported service.
The location and the staff member who handled it.
A provider reference or receipt number where one exists.
The resulting cash and float position, where the system can calculate it.
Totals are a summary, not a record. If the only entry for the day is a lump sum, a customer dispute or a staff query cannot be investigated later.
Keep business money separate from personal money
Reconcile at closing, not at the end of the month
Count the cashCount the physical cash in the presence of a second person where possible, and write the figure down before checking the expected balance.
Count the physical cash in the presence of a second person where possible, and write the figure down before checking the expected balance.
Check the floatCompare the electronic balance with the platform or provider record. Note any transaction still pending.
Compare the electronic balance with the platform or provider record. Note any transaction still pending.
Explain every differenceA difference is not automatically a loss. It may be an unrecorded charge, a pending reversal or a transaction entered twice. Record the explanation and who gave it.
A difference is not automatically a loss. It may be an unrecorded charge, a pending reversal or a transaction entered twice. Record the explanation and who gave it.
Close the dayLock the day's records, carry the closing position to the next opening, and keep the summary with the transaction detail.
Lock the day's records, carry the closing position to the next opening, and keep the summary with the transaction detail.
Handle susu collections as a separate ledger
A collector's route changes. Customers miss a day. A partial payment is agreed. The record must allow those realities without losing the link between the customer and the money.
Review the week, not only the day
This review is where patterns appear. A daily difference may be an error. The same difference every Friday is a process problem.
Recording only the day's total, which makes individual transactions impossible to trace.
Letting staff share a login, which removes accountability without improving speed.
Treating float and cash as one number.
Failing to record reversals and pending transactions.
Keeping customer data in a personal phone with no backup and no access control.
Reconciling only when something goes wrong.
Good recordkeeping does not make a business slower. It makes the difficult conversation shorter, because the answer is already written down.

Stock control for electrical shops: item codes, counts and accountability
How electrical retailers can organise item codes, receiving, transfers, pricing and cycle counts so that the stock record matches the shelf.
By BloomCore Technologies · 9 November 2026 · 9 min read
The aim of stock control is not a perfect spreadsheet. It is a record that answers three questions quickly: what is here, where is it, and who moved it?
Give every item a stable code
Record the unit of measure with the code. Cable may be stocked in rolls and sold in metres. A code that does not state the unit invites a costly conversion error.
One code per sellable variant, not one code per supplier invoice line.
A description a new staff member can match to the shelf.
A unit of measure and, where relevant, the pack size.
A reorder level based on normal sales, not on a guess.
Where the same item comes from two suppliers at different costs, keep the cost attached to the receipt. A single average cost hides which supplier is actually cheaper.
Update the record at the point of sale
For items sold by length or partial quantity, record the quantity sold rather than the number of pieces. A roll of cable that leaves the store should reduce the metres, not the roll count.
Decide who may change a price. Record the old price, the new price, the date and the person who approved it. This is not bureaucracy; it is the difference between a discount and an unexplained margin
Keep a current price list where staff can see it. If a price is negotiated for a customer, record the reason and the approver.
At the start of a shift, record the opening float. At the end, count the cash and compare it with sales, refunds and any expenses paid from the till. The person responsible should sign or confirm the

A practical, indicator-first method for turning a term scheme of learning into weekly lesson plans that a teacher can actually teach and defend.
By BloomCore Technologies · 9 November 2026 · 9 min read
1. Read the scheme as a sequence, not a list
2. Map the weeks to real teaching time
3. Turn each indicator into one lesson objective

4. Choose teaching and learning resources that exist
Where a resource is scarce, design the lesson around groups or a demonstration. Record who carries what, so the activity does not collapse at the start of the period.

This small habit is what turns a template into professional judgement. The scheme stays stable; the plan learns from the classroom.

Copying the content standard into the objective. A standard describes the destination; an objective describes what this lesson will produce.
Planning three indicators for one period. Depth beats coverage when the indicator will be assessed.

Leaving assessment to the end of the term. Build a small evidence point into every lesson.
Rewriting the whole scheme each week. Keep the scheme, adjust the plan.

Recordkeeping for a mobile money business: a daily routine that works
A daily routine for mobile money agents and multi-location operators: opening position, transaction records, float and reconciliation.
By BloomCore Technologies · 9 November 2026 · 10 min read
The routine below is deliberately ordinary. It is designed to be repeated every day by people who are busy serving customers, not by an accountant at the end of the month.
If the business runs several locations, each location needs its own opening position. A single organisation-wide total hides the branch that is short.
Record the transaction, not just the total
For each transaction, capture enough detail to answer a customer query without guesswork:
Customer name or a consistent customer reference.
Transaction type: deposit, withdrawal, transfer, bill payment, airtime, or another supported service.
The location and the staff member who handled it.
A provider reference or receipt number where one exists.
The resulting cash and float position, where the system can calculate it.
Totals are a summary, not a record. If the only entry for the day is a lump sum, a customer dispute or a staff query cannot be investigated later.
Keep business money separate from personal money
Reconcile at closing, not at the end of the month
Count the cashCount the physical cash in the presence of a second person where possible, and write the figure down before checking the expected balance.

Check the floatCompare the electronic balance with the platform or provider record. Note any transaction still pending.

Explain every differenceA difference is not automatically a loss. It may be an unrecorded charge, a pending reversal or a transaction entered twice. Record the explanation and who gave it.

Handle susu collections as a separate ledger
A collector's route changes. Customers miss a day. A partial payment is agreed. The record must allow those realities without losing the link between the customer and the money.
Review the week, not only the day
This review is where patterns appear. A daily difference may be an error. The same difference every Friday is a process problem.
Recording only the day's total, which makes individual transactions impossible to trace.
Letting staff share a login, which removes accountability without improving speed.
Treating float and cash as one number.
Failing to record reversals and pending transactions.
Keeping customer data in a personal phone with no backup and no access control.
Reconciling only when something goes wrong.
Good recordkeeping does not make a business slower. It makes the difficult conversation shorter, because the answer is already written down.

Stock control for electrical shops: item codes, counts and accountability
How electrical retailers can organise item codes, receiving, transfers, pricing and cycle counts so that the stock record matches the shelf.
By BloomCore Technologies · 9 November 2026 · 9 min read
The aim of stock control is not a perfect spreadsheet. It is a record that answers three questions quickly: what is here, where is it, and who moved it?
Give every item a stable code
Record the unit of measure with the code. Cable may be stocked in rolls and sold in metres. A code that does not state the unit invites a costly conversion error.
One code per sellable variant, not one code per supplier invoice line.
A description a new staff member can match to the shelf.
A unit of measure and, where relevant, the pack size.
A reorder level based on normal sales, not on a guess.
Where the same item comes from two suppliers at different costs, keep the cost attached to the receipt. A single average cost hides which supplier is actually cheaper.
Update the record at the point of sale
For items sold by length or partial quantity, record the quantity sold rather than the number of pieces. A roll of cable that leaves the store should reduce the metres, not the roll count.
Decide who may change a price. Record the old price, the new price, the date and the person who approved it. This is not bureaucracy; it is the difference between a discount and an unexplained margin
Keep a current price list where staff can see it. If a price is negotiated for a customer, record the reason and the approver.

A difference is information. Record it, explain it and look for a pattern. Punishing every small difference without investigating it teaches staff to hide differences instead of reporting them.

Monthly category countCount one full category, such as breakers or sockets. This catches mis-picks and units errors without stopping the whole shop.
